title: The Wind Cries Typhoid Mary
summary: Josh and Chuck open with the late-19th-century horse manure problem in New York City and the Department of Health's street-cleaning crews, then tell the story of Typhoid Mary (Mary Mallon). They cover typhoid fever and its toll, the 1906 Oyster Bay outbreak at the Thompson family home, sanitation engineer George Soper's investigation, Mallon's forced confinement on North Brother Island, her court case and the "Typhoid Mary" nickname, her release on condition she stop cooking, her return to cooking under an assumed name at Sloane Hospital, and the civil liberties debate. The episode closes with a listener mail correction about Moon facts (tidal locking, the far side, tides) and sign-off.

segments.title: Typhoid fever and its toll
segments.summary: The hosts describe typhoid fever's symptoms, its spread through contaminated hands and uncooked food, its high historical death rate, and famous victims including Mary Todd Lincoln and Wilbur Wright.

segments.title: Oyster Bay outbreak and Soper's investigation
segments.summary: In summer 1906 typhoid broke out at the Thompson family's house in Oyster Bay. Sanitation engineer George Soper was hired to find the source, and after interviewing household staff he learned that former cook Mary Mallon had worked for several families with outbreaks and served uncooked peaches and ice cream.

segments.title: Healthy carriers and Mary Mallon's background
segments.summary: The hosts explain the healthy carrier concept, why Soper believed Mallon was one, and describe her Irish background, her rise as a domestic cook, and her hostile reaction when Soper asked for samples.

segments.title: Mallon's capture and North Brother Island
segments.summary: Health Commissioner Herman Biggs ordered Mallon seized. After a long search she was taken to a quarantine hospital, tested, offered a deal to give up cooking, refused, and was confined on North Brother Island, where she believed the department had a vendetta against her.

segments.title: Court case, nickname, and release
segments.summary: Mallon's private lab tests disagreed with the department's results. A court hearing followed, the court ruled her a public health threat, and newspapers, reportedly helped by William Randolph Hearst, gave her the Typhoid Mary nickname. After about three years a new commissioner released her and offered her a laundry job, and she later vanished from contact.

segments.title: Return to cooking at Sloane Hospital
segments.summary: Years later, under an assumed name, Mallon cooked at Sloane Hospital for maternity patients. Doctors, nurses and others fell ill and Soper was called back, recognized her, and she surrendered. The hosts note about fifty-two cases and three deaths were attributed to her.

segments.title: Legacy, civil liberties debate, and Typhoid Mary's character
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether Mallon was a bad person, the tension between individual civil rights and public health, and the idea that a different first meeting might have changed the outcome. They mention the Nova documentary and the How Stuff Works article.
